title: Superset vs Dragonfly v2.0.2 vs upstream Valkey

df.label: Dragonfly v2.0.2
df.commit: official aarch64 release binary (tarball sha256 matches the GitHub release digest), default flags, snapshots off

views.tab: Dragonfly's connection shape (1152 at P1, 256 at P16)

instances.server: c8g.metal-24xl (Graviton4), the server process confined with taskset to the layout's CPUs; every thread pinned to its slot; NIC IRQs round-robin over the irq CPUs
instances.generators: two c8g.metal-24xl hosts in the same AZ and placement group running memtier; round trip about 0.11 ms to the server

views.method: Cores = total CPUs the server may use (main, IO threads, poller, NIC IRQs, bio/jemalloc; Dragonfly: proactors and helpers), layout per core count listed below. memtier, 128 B values, 1M keys, P1 and P16, total connections 1152 at P1 and 256 at P16 (Dragonfly's benchmark guide uses about 1,200 and 300), 10 s window, 3 reps per build, build order rotating per rep, server restarted per rep. 840 reps. Dragonfly gets the same IRQ CPUs as Valkey and one proactor on every other CPU. Better/worse: medians more than 5% apart with no rep overlap.
caveats: Dragonfly ran the v2.0.2 release binary with default flags. A probe of its threading, I/O-backend and sharding flags at 8 cores found nothing faster than the defaults. From 4 cores up every proactor is 100% busy.
At 2 cores both CPUs also take the NIC interrupts, so no engine's threads reach 100%: Dragonfly's proactors run at 78-94% at P1, and the rest of the CPU goes to interrupt handling.

At 4 cores and P1 the single IRQ CPU is 100% busy for superset and Dragonfly, so those cells are limited by the network path. Dragonfly also runs a proactor on the fourth CPU, which the Valkey builds keep for bio and leave mostly idle at P1. Dragonfly leads superset by 6-12% there.
At 8 cores and P1 Dragonfly leads superset by 6-9% on SET, SISMEMBER and HSET and ties on GET and 80/20.

At 16 cores superset's io_epoll poller shares the last IO thread's CPU (about 50% each). Every phase barrier waits on that thread, so the other IO threads run at about 83% busy. Superset at P1 is 0.64-0.82x Dragonfly and 0.84x upstream on SET. A layout that gives the poller its own CPU was not measured.

Upstream turns IO threads on by demand. At 16 cores one of its 9 IO threads stayed idle (shown as W0) while its main thread was 100% busy, so upstream is main-bound there, not limited by the load generator.
Per-request latency in every cell is well above the 0.11 ms round trip to the generators, and no cell exceeded the NIC allowance.
Superset (ss) and superset-frontier (fr) are within 2% of each other except at P16: frontier is 3-4% lower on GET at 2, 4 and 8 cores and 9% lower on SISMEMBER at 8 cores.

views.tab: High connection count (9,600 at P1, 2,304 at P16)

instances.server: c8g.metal-24xl (Graviton4), restricted with taskset to the N-core layout below
instances.generators: two c8g.metal-24xl hosts in the same AZ running memtier; round trips 0.11 ms and 0.23 ms, far below per-request latency in every cell
instances.layout at N cores: N/2 cores (min 1) for NIC IRQs, round-robin; N worker cores (Valkey: main + N-1 IO threads; Dragonfly: N proactor threads; superset's io_epoll poller also on the last worker core); one spare core for bio and jemalloc

views.method: memtier, 128 B values, 1M keys, P1 and P16, 10 s measurement window, 3 reps per build, build order rotating per rep, server restarted per rep. 672 reps, 0 failed. Better/worse: medians more than 5% apart with no rep overlap. Latency is closed-loop client latency, median of per-second percentiles. Originally published as 2/4/8/16 cores, which counted only worker CPUs (main + IO threads, or proactors); relabelled to total CPUs, numbers unchanged.
caveats: Dragonfly ran with default flags and was not tuned. From 4 cores up every proactor thread is 95-100% busy, so those numbers are its CPU-bound throughput for this setup (memtier, about 2,400 connections at P16).
At 2 cores and P1 Dragonfly is unbalanced: one proactor about 99% busy, the other about 50%. Part of the 2.4-5x lead there is that imbalance, not CPU.

At 8 and 16 cores superset's io_epoll poller shares the last worker core with the last IO thread (about 50% each), and every phase barrier waits on that thread, so superset numbers there are a lower bound for this layout.
That shared core is the main reason superset trails upstream on SET P1 at 8 cores (1.01M vs 1.42M), the one cell from 4 cores up where it loses to upstream.
Upstream's IO threads sit idle at P16 because upstream is main-bound there; that is not a load-generator limit.
ENA: the NIC bandwidth allowance was exceeded in the window (MGET/MSET at P16 from 4 cores up), so the cell is a floor. IRQ: an IRQ core was above 90% busy, so the network path may be the limit.

This shape uses about 8x the connections of Dragonfly's benchmark guide. Dragonfly's cost per command roughly doubles from 1,152 to 9,600 connections (last-level cache misses per GET rise 5.4x), so this view understates Dragonfly; see the other view.

correction: Correction, 2026-10-28. The first version of this page (2026-10-27) ran every build at 9,600 connections at P1 and 2,304 at P16, about 8x what Dragonfly's benchmark guide uses. Dragonfly slows down sharply as connections go up, so that run understated it, and its headline that superset beat Dragonfly in every cell does not hold: at Dragonfly's shape Dragonfly leads superset at P1 on single-key commands at 4, 8 and 16 cores. The first version also counted only worker threads as cores. This version adds a full rerun at Dragonfly's connection shape (1,152 at P1, 256 at P16), where cores means every CPU the server may use and the layout is stated for each core count, and adds the superset-frontier build. The original data is kept as the second view, relabelled to 4, 7, 13 and 25 total cores with its numbers unchanged. The scaling, ratio, table and method sections did not render on the first version; they render now.
